avoid.reason: Caution beyond the French Quarter/Garden District; parts of Central City and the 7th/9th Ward are high-crime — avoid quiet streets at night.

hood_desc: The historic 18th-century heart of the city, a walkable grid of iron-lace balconies, Jackson Square, Bourbon Street bars, and Creole restaurants; the classic first-timer base where everything is on foot.
A colorful bohemian neighborhood just downriver of the Quarter, home to Frenchmen Street's live-jazz clubs and Creole cottages; the local pick for authentic music nights.
Tree-lined avenues of grand antebellum mansions, Magazine Street shopping, and the St. Charles streetcar; a genteel, quieter area perfect for strolling and Southern charm.
The revitalized former warehouse quarter, now dense with museums like the National WWII Museum and the CAC, galleries, and stylish hotels; a central, cultured base close to the CBD.
An arty, pastel-hued riverside neighborhood of muralled cottages, indie cafes, and Crescent Park; increasingly hip and creative, drawing a younger, local-leaning crowd.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink.

transit.pay: Tap the RTA GoMobile app, a contactless card, or pay exact cash on board. A single streetcar, bus, or ferry ride is $1.25; a 1-day Jazzy Pass is $3 and covers unlimited rides on all three.
transit.hours: The St. Charles streetcar runs 24 hours; the Canal and Riverfront lines and most buses run roughly 5am to midnight, with reduced overnight service.

food.name: Gumbo
food.desc: Dark-roux stew of seafood or chicken and andouille sausage, thickened with okra or file and ladled over rice. The city's defining bowl.

places.name: Dooky Chase's Restaurant
places.note: Leah Chase's Creole landmark; the Holy Thursday gumbo z'herbes is legendary.

places.name: Gumbo Shop
places.note: Courtyard institution on St Peter serving seafood okra and chicken andouille gumbo daily.

places.name: Li'l Dizzy's Cafe
places.note: Creole soul-food room where gumbo comes alongside famous fried chicken.

food.name: Po'boy
food.desc: Crackly Leidenheimer French bread stuffed with fried shrimp, oysters or slow-roast beef and gravy, dressed with lettuce, tomato and mayo.

places.name: Parkway Bakery & Tavern
places.note: Open since 1911; the roast beef po'boy is the benchmark and the patio is always busy.

places.name: Domilise's Po-Boys
places.note: Family-run corner shop since 1918, famous for fried shrimp on hot-buttered bread.

places.name: Mahony's Po-Boy Shop
places.note: Modern shop known for fried shrimp with hot sausage and thick-cut sandwiches.

food.name: Beignets
food.desc: Square pillows of fried dough buried under powdered sugar, eaten hot with chicory coffee at any hour of the day or night.

places.name: Cafe du Monde
places.note: Open since 1862 and around the clock; three beignets and a cafe au lait is the ritual.

places.name: Cafe Beignet
places.note: Smaller courtyard cafes with live jazz and shorter queues than Cafe du Monde.

places.name: Loretta's Authentic Pralines
places.note: Praline-stuffed beignets from a Black-owned French Market favourite.

food.name: Jambalaya
food.desc: Rice cooked in the pot with the trinity, tomato, andouille and shrimp or chicken, so every grain takes on the seasoning.

places.name: Coop's Place
places.note: Dive-bar kitchen on Decatur famous for rabbit and sausage jambalaya; adults only.

places.name: Mother's Restaurant
places.note: Cafeteria-style since 1938, doing jambalaya alongside its Ferdi special po'boy.

places.name: Jacques-Imo's Cafe
places.note: Eccentric Creole-soul room next to the Maple Leaf Bar; go early or expect a wait.

food.name: Muffuletta
food.desc: Round sesame loaf layered with mortadella, salami, provolone and marinated olive salad. A Sicilian-New Orleans invention sold by the half.

places.name: Central Grocery
places.note: The 1906 grocery that invented the sandwich; back open after long storm repairs.

places.name: Napoleon House
places.note: Historic bar serving its muffuletta warm, with a Pimm's Cup in the courtyard.

places.name: Cochon Butcher
places.note: Butcher-shop sandwich counter with a house-cured take on the classic.

food.name: Crawfish boil
food.desc: Louisiana crawfish boiled with cayenne, lemon, garlic, corn and potatoes and dumped on newspaper. Peak season runs roughly February to May.

places.name: Bevi Seafood Co
places.note: Local favourite for boiled crawfish by the pound plus a strong seafood po'boy.

places.name: Big Fisherman Seafood
places.note: Old-school boiling house selling hot crawfish to go all through the season.

places.name: Frankie & Johnny's
places.note: Neighbourhood seafood joint since 1942 with boils and fried platters.

food.name: Sazerac
food.desc: Rye whiskey or cognac stirred with Peychaud's bitters and sugar in an absinthe-rinsed glass. Louisiana's official cocktail.

places.name: Sazerac Bar
places.note: Art-deco bar with Paul Ninas murals; the classic place to order the drink by name.

places.name: Jewel of the South
places.note: Award-winning cocktail room in a Creole cottage courtyard, strong on historic recipes.

places.name: Napoleon House
places.note: Peeling-plaster bar from 1797 pouring Sazeracs and Pimm's Cups all day.

food.name: Chicory cafe au lait
food.desc: Dark-roast coffee cut with roasted chicory root and equal parts hot milk, a Civil War thrift habit that became the local morning standard.

places.name: Cafe du Monde
places.note: The archetype; order it with beignets and let the powdered sugar fall where it will.

places.name: Cafe Beignet
places.note: Quieter courtyard alternative with the same chicory blend and live music.

places.name: CC's Coffee House
places.note: Louisiana-born chain; reliable chicory au lait away from the tourist queues.

landmarks: French Quarter (Vieux Carré)
The historic heart of New Orleans, packed with colorful Creole cottages, wrought-iron balconies, and the sounds of live jazz spilling into the street.
Jackson Square
A picture-perfect plaza framed by St. Louis Cathedral, street artists, and fortune tellers, forming the postcard image of New Orleans.
St. Louis Cathedral
The oldest continuously operating Catholic cathedral in the United States, its triple spires anchoring the French Quarter skyline.
Bourbon Street
The legendary, neon-lit strip famous for its raucous nightlife, live music clubs, and non-stop French Quarter energy.
Garden District
A leafy, elegant neighborhood of antebellum mansions and oak-canopied streets showcasing New Orleans' grand Southern architecture.
Frenchmen Street
The go-to strip for authentic local jazz and blues clubs, favored by musicians and locals over the touristy Bourbon Street scene.
Louisiana Superdome (Caesars Superdome)
The massive gleaming dome that dominates the skyline and is a symbol of the city's resilience and love of football.
St. Louis Cemetery No. 1
An atmospheric 'city of the dead' filled with ornate above-ground tombs, including the reputed grave of voodoo queen Marie Laveau.
Mississippi Riverfront & Steamboat Natchez
A scenic walk along the Mississippi River where the historic steamboat Natchez paddles by, evoking the city's riverboat heritage.
National WWII Museum
An acclaimed museum with immersive exhibits and dramatic architecture chronicling the American experience in World War II.

train.note: The Union Passenger Terminal on Loyola Avenue, walkable from the French Quarter and on the streetcar line, is unusually well served for the South: the City of New Orleans north to Memphis and Chicago, the Crescent east to Birmingham, Atlanta, Washington and New York, the Sunset Limited west to Houston, San Antonio, Tucson and Los Angeles three times a week, and the new Mardi Gras Service which launched on 18 August 2025 running along the Gulf coast to Mobile, Alabama via Bay St Louis, Gulfport, Biloxi and Pascagoula. The Gulf coast route had been out of service since Hurricane Katrina, so its return is recent news worth checking timetables for. No international trains serve Louisiana. Sleepers on the three long-distance trains are worth booking months ahead for Mardi Gras and Jazz Fest.

bus.note: There are no international coach services from New Orleans. Conveniently, Greyhound (https://www.greyhound.com/) and Megabus (https://us.megabus.com/) both operate from the same Union Passenger Terminal as the trains, so bus and rail share one central building a short walk or streetcar ride from the French Quarter. Typical journey times are around eight hours to Memphis, nine to Atlanta, six to Houston and two to Baton Rouge. Tickets are sold online and at counters in the terminal.

intl.to: Algiers Point (USA) - departs the ferry terminal at the foot of Canal Street
Lower Algiers (USA) - departs Chalmette, downriver in St Bernard Parish

ferry.note: The Canal Street to Algiers Point ferry is a genuine piece of public transport and one of the best cheap views in the city, crossing the Mississippi in under ten minutes; it carries pedestrians and bicycles but no cars. The Chalmette to Lower Algiers ferry further downriver does take vehicles. Both are run by the RTA on regular daily schedules and can be suspended in high water or fog. There are no international or long-distance ferries - the port handles cargo and cruise ships.

half.name: Oak Alley Plantation
half.blurb: A 19th-century plantation house approached by a quarter-mile alley of live oak trees planted a century before it.

half.name: Honey Island Swamp
half.blurb: A cypress-tupelo swamp on the Pearl River, explored by boat tours that spot alligators and wading birds.

half.name: Baton Rouge
half.blurb: Louisiana's state capital, with the 34-story Louisiana State Capitol building and the old capitol's Gothic Revival architecture.

full.name: Lafayette (Cajun Country)
full.blurb: The center of Cajun culture in Louisiana, with zydeco music venues and Vermilionville's living-history Cajun village.
